Brown
broun
adj. (dusky; in the Authorized Version the colour of the sheep Jacob took for his hire from Laban)
Old English brun, dark, dusky. The Hebrew chum means scorched or dark, and it appears only in the Jacob and Laban account, where the colour of a beast decided a man's wages.

Biblical Definition

Every occurrence of this word is in one chapter of Genesis, and the whole chapter turns on a bargain about colour. Jacob names his own wages: “I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire” (Gen 30:32). Ordinary Near Eastern sheep were white and goats were dark, so Jacob asked for the exceptions — the least likely animals, which is why Laban agreed at once. Laban then removed those very animals: “he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted… and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons” (Gen 30:35), putting three days' journey between them and Jacob. Jacob worked with what was left: “And Jacob did separate the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the ringstraked, and all the brown in the flock of Laban” (Gen 30:40). The increase came, and Jacob's own summary in the next chapter gives the true account of it: “Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” (Gen 31:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines brown as a dusky color, inclining to redness; and notes it as compounded of black and red, or of black, red and yellow.

BROWN, a. Dusky; of a dark or dusky color, inclining to redness.

All the brown cattle among the sheep. Gen. xxx.

BROWN, n. A dark dusky color inclining to redness.

BROWNNESS, n. A brown color.

Key Scripture

Gen 30:32 — "I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire."

Gen 30:35 — "And he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, and all the she goats that were speckled and spotted, and every one that had some white in it, and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons."

Gen 30:40 — "And Jacob did separate the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the ringstraked, and all the brown in the flock of Laban; and he put his own flocks by themselves, and put them not unto Laban's cattle."

Gen 31:9 — "Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me."

Modern Corruption

Jacob's prosperity is credited either to his cleverness with rods or to folk superstition, while Jacob himself and the angel in the next chapter credit it to God.

expand to see more

Genesis 30 is one of the passages most often used to prove that the patriarchal narratives preserve primitive folk belief — peeled rods set in the watering troughs so that the flocks would conceive striped young. The text is more careful than its critics. It reports what Jacob did without ever saying that the rods produced the result, and Genesis 31 supplies the explanation from two sources: the angel of God in a dream, who told Jacob what he had seen of Laban's dealings, and Jacob's own confession that God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me. The narrative allows Jacob his scheming, records it without approval, and then removes the credit from it entirely. That is the pattern of the whole Jacob story, in which a man contrives at every turn and is prospered in spite of his contrivances.

Laban is the other lesson and he is the more common figure. He agreed to the wage, then went the same day and removed every animal that would have paid it, and set three days between Jacob and the flock. Genesis says he changed Jacob's wages ten times. This is the ordinary conduct of an employer who has power and no fear of God, and Scripture is not neutral about it: the law commands that the hired man's wage not stay overnight, and James says the hire of the labourers kept back by fraud crieth, and the cries are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth. The brown sheep are a small detail in a long account, and what they mark is a bargain honestly made and dishonestly kept — with the outcome, in the end, entirely out of the dishonest man's hands.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chum (H2345), dark, dusky, brown — found only in Genesis 30; with naqod (H5348), speckled, and talu (H2921), spotted, the other terms of the bargain.

expand to see more

Hebrew chum (H2345) — scorched, dark brown; used only of Laban's sheep; Genesis 30:32, Genesis 30:40.

Hebrew naqod (H5348) — speckled; the goats of the same bargain; Genesis 30:32.

Hebrew aqod (H6124) — ringstraked, banded at the ankles; Genesis 30:35.

Hebrew sakar (H7939) — hire, wages; of such shall be my hire; Genesis 30:32.

Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to strip away, to deliver; God hath taken away the cattle of your father; Genesis 31:9.

Usage

"“All the brown cattle among the sheep… of such shall be my hire” — a wage set in the unlikely animals."

"“He removed that day… all the brown among the sheep” — the bargain kept in word and broken in fact."

"“God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” — the credit removed from the rods."
